entries.meaning: Attack has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Two men attacked him outside the bar.
A wounded animal will attack anyone who comes close.
The base was attacked twice in the same week.
Don't attack the person; argue with the idea.
The senator attacked the plan as a handout to big banks.
Newspapers have been attacking the mayor for weeks.
Let's attack the hardest problem first.
She attacked the pile of dishes as soon as the guests left.
They're attacking the backlog one order at a time.
The virus attacks the nervous system.
The disease attacked his joints first.
Termites had been attacking the beams for years before anyone looked.

senses.head: To use violence against a person, place, or army in order to hurt them or take control
examples: Two men attacked him outside the bar.
A wounded animal will attack anyone who comes close.
The base was attacked twice in the same week.

senses.head: To criticize someone or something strongly and publicly
examples: Don't attack the person; argue with the idea.
The senator attacked the plan as a handout to big banks.
Newspapers have been attacking the mayor for weeks.

senses.head: To begin work on something with great energy
examples: Let's attack the hardest problem first.
She attacked the pile of dishes as soon as the guests left.
They're attacking the backlog one order at a time.

senses.head: Of a disease, chemical, or insect, to damage something by acting on it
examples: The virus attacks the nervous system.
The disease attacked his joints first.
Termites had been attacking the beams for years before anyone looked.

entries.русский: нападать, напасть; атаковать; критиковать, обрушиваться с критикой; нападать (словесно); энергично браться за, приниматься за, взяться; поражать, поразить (о болезни, вредителях)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they attacked the village), intransitive (the enemy attacked at dawn)

entries.meaning: To attack someone violently, especially in a way that is a crime. ---
examples: He was arrested for assaulting a police officer.
Two teenagers assaulted the driver and took his keys.
Nobody who assaults a stranger on the street walks away free.
entries.contrast: The silent au sounds like aw: uh-SAWLT, never "uh-SALT".

entries.meaning: To attack someone suddenly from a hidden position. ---
examples: Rebels ambushed the convoy on a mountain road.
They planned to ambush the patrol at the bridge.
The soldiers had been ambushed before they reached the border.
entries.contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: ambushes.

entries.meaning: Invade has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The Romans invaded Britain almost two thousand years ago.
No small country expects a neighbor to invade it overnight.
The island has been invaded three times in its history.
The photographers invaded her privacy at the hospital.
Reading someone's texts invades their privacy.
He has never invaded his kids' privacy that way.

senses.head: To enter a country or area with an army in order to take control of it
examples: The Romans invaded Britain almost two thousand years ago.
No small country expects a neighbor to invade it overnight.
The island has been invaded three times in its history.

senses.head: To intrude on something private, especially a person's privacy
examples: The photographers invaded her privacy at the hospital.
Reading someone's texts invades their privacy.
He has never invaded his kids' privacy that way.

entries.русский: вторгаться, вторгнуться; захватывать; вторгаться, вторгнуться (в личную жизнь); нарушать (неприкосновенность)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (invade a country), intransitive (the army invaded in spring)
entries.contrast: No preposition after it: invaded Poland, not "invaded into Poland".

entries.meaning: Raid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Police raided the warehouse just before dawn.
Agents raid the club almost every summer.
The apartment had already been raided twice that year.
The kids raided the fridge the minute they got home.
He had to raid his savings to pay for the repair.
The pension fund had been raided years before anyone noticed.

senses.head: To make a sudden attack on a place, or to enter it suddenly as police looking for something
examples: Police raided the warehouse just before dawn.
Agents raid the club almost every summer.
The apartment had already been raided twice that year.

senses.head: To go into a place and help yourself to what is in it, especially food or money
examples: The kids raided the fridge the minute they got home.
He had to raid his savings to pay for the repair.
The pension fund had been raided years before anyone noticed.

entries.русский: совершать налёт; устраивать облаву; опустошать, опустошить (холодильник); залезать, залезть (в сбережения, фонд)

entries.meaning: Bombard has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The artillery bombarded the city for six days.
Ships out at sea began to bombard the coast.
Reporters kept bombarding the general with questions.
Reporters bombarded her with questions about the deal.
We are bombarded with ads from the moment we wake up.
Stop bombarding me with texts; I'll answer tonight.

senses.head: To attack a place continuously with bombs or heavy gunfire
examples: The artillery bombarded the city for six days.
Ships out at sea began to bombard the coast.
Reporters kept bombarding the general with questions.

senses.head: To direct a great many questions, messages, or demands at someone
examples: Reporters bombarded her with questions about the deal.
We are bombarded with ads from the moment we wake up.
Stop bombarding me with texts; I'll answer tonight.

entries.contrast: Unlike bomb /bɑːm/, the second b here is pronounced: bahm-BAHRD.

entries.meaning: Storm has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Commandos stormed the embassy at three in the morning.
Crowds threatened to storm the gates of the palace.
The prison was stormed by troops after the riot spread.
He tends to storm around the kitchen when he is angry.
She stormed into the principal's office.
He came storming past me without a word.
It is supposed to storm tonight.
It stormed all weekend, so the game was canceled.
It has been storming since dawn.

senses.head: To attack a building or position suddenly and in force
examples: Commandos stormed the embassy at three in the morning.
Crowds threatened to storm the gates of the palace.
The prison was stormed by troops after the riot spread.

senses.head: To go somewhere in a noisy, angry way
examples: He tends to storm around the kitchen when he is angry.
She stormed into the principal's office.
He came storming past me without a word.

senses.head: To rain, snow, or blow violently
examples: It is supposed to storm tonight.
It stormed all weekend, so the game was canceled.
It has been storming since dawn.

entries.русский: штурмовать, брать штурмом; врываться, ворваться; проноситься в ярости; бушевать (о непогоде); разыграться (о буре)

entries.meaning: Besiege has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The army besieged the city for nine months.
No modern general wants to besiege a place that size.
The fortress had been besieged twice before it fell.
Reporters besieged the family's front porch.
The office is besieged with calls every time prices change.
Fans have been besieging the station with requests all week.

senses.head: To surround a town or fort with an army so that nobody can get in or out
examples: The army besieged the city for nine months.
No modern general wants to besiege a place that size.
The fortress had been besieged twice before it fell.

senses.head: To crowd around someone, or to overwhelm them with requests and questions
examples: Reporters besieged the family's front porch.
The office is besieged with calls every time prices change.
Fans have been besieging the station with requests all week.

entries.contrast: Spelled -ie-: besiege, besieged — not "beseige".

entries.meaning: Conquer has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Spain conquered most of South America in a century.
An empire that cannot feed itself cannot conquer anyone.
Half of Europe had been conquered by the end of that year.
Nobody conquers jet lag on the first day.
She conquered her fear of flying last year.
The disease has not been conquered yet.

senses.head: To take control of a country or people by force
examples: Spain conquered most of South America in a century.
An empire that cannot feed itself cannot conquer anyone.
Half of Europe had been conquered by the end of that year.

senses.head: To succeed in dealing with a fear, a problem, or a difficulty
examples: Nobody conquers jet lag on the first day.
She conquered her fear of flying last year.
The disease has not been conquered yet.

entries.русский: завоёвывать, завоевать; покорять, покорить; побеждать, побороть; преодолевать, преодолеть (страх)
entries.contrast: The qu here is just /k/: KAHNG-kur, not "KON-kwer".

entries.meaning: Defeat has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The rebels defeated a much larger army.
A smaller force can defeat a big one on the right ground.
Their team has never been defeated at home.
Driving to the gym defeats the purpose of exercising.
The extra fee defeated the whole point of the discount.
Bad weather has defeated every attempt to reach the summit.

senses.head: To beat an enemy or opponent in a battle, election, or game
examples: The rebels defeated a much larger army.
A smaller force can defeat a big one on the right ground.
Their team has never been defeated at home.

senses.head: To make a plan, a purpose, or an effort fail
examples: Driving to the gym defeats the purpose of exercising.
The extra fee defeated the whole point of the discount.
Bad weather has defeated every attempt to reach the summit.

entries.русский: побеждать, победить; наносить поражение; сводить на нет, срывать, сорвать

entries.meaning: Overpower has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Three guards overpowered the man at the door.
He is strong enough to overpower anyone in the room.
The pilot was overpowered by two passengers.
Too much garlic overpowers the sauce.
Her perfume overpowered the whole elevator.
The chili was overpowering everything else in the bowl.

senses.head: To beat someone by being physically stronger than they are
examples: Three guards overpowered the man at the door.
He is strong enough to overpower anyone in the room.
The pilot was overpowered by two passengers.

senses.head: Of a taste or smell, to be so strong that it hides everything else
examples: Too much garlic overpowers the sauce.
Her perfume overpowered the whole elevator.
The chili was overpowering everything else in the bowl.

entries.русский: одолевать, одолеть; пересиливать; перебивать (вкус, запах), заглушать

entries.meaning: To be greater in number than another group. ---
examples: The defenders were outnumbered five to one.
Police outnumbered the protesters on the square.
Any army that outnumbers you still has to feed itself.

entries.meaning: Punch has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He punched the other driver in the face.
Don't punch a wall when you are angry.
The boxer kept punching until the bell rang.
The conductor punched our tickets.
Punch three holes along the side of the box.
The card had been punched in the wrong place.

senses.head: To hit someone hard with your closed fist
examples: He punched the other driver in the face.
Don't punch a wall when you are angry.
The boxer kept punching until the bell rang.

senses.head: To make a hole in paper, a card, or thin material with a tool
examples: The conductor punched our tickets.
Punch three holes along the side of the box.
The card had been punched in the wrong place.

entries.русский: бить кулаком, ударить кулаком; пробивать, пробить (отверстие); компостировать (билет)
entries.contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: punches.
entries.phrasal verbs: punch in · punch in · punch out · punch out · punch up

entries.meaning: Kick has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Somebody kicked the door until the lock broke.
The horse will kick if you stand behind it.
He was kicking the fence out of sheer frustration.
He finally kicked the habit at fifty.
It took her two years to kick her soda habit.
He has kicked worse addictions than this one.

senses.head: To hit someone or something with your foot
examples: Somebody kicked the door until the lock broke.
The horse will kick if you stand behind it.
He was kicking the fence out of sheer frustration.

senses.head: To succeed in stopping a bad habit or an addiction
examples: He finally kicked the habit at fifty.
It took her two years to kick her soda habit.
He has kicked worse addictions than this one.

entries.русский: пинать, пнуть; ударять ногой; бросать, бросить (вредную привычку); завязать (с чем-л.)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (kick the door), intransitive (the horse kicks)
entries.phrasal verbs: kick around · kick back · kick in · kick in · kick off · kick out

entries.meaning: Slap has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She slapped him and walked out.
Never slap a child across the face.
He was slapped twice before he understood she meant it.
Regulators slapped the bank with a record fine.
The city will slap a fee on plastic bags.
He has been slapped with a lawsuit.

senses.head: To hit someone with the flat, open palm of your hand
examples: She slapped him and walked out.
Never slap a child across the face.
He was slapped twice before he understood she meant it.

senses.head: To impose a fine, tax, or penalty on someone, especially suddenly
examples: Regulators slapped the bank with a record fine.
The city will slap a fee on plastic bags.
He has been slapped with a lawsuit.

entries.русский: шлёпать, шлёпнуть; давать пощёчину; налагать (штраф, пошлину), наложить; влепить (штраф)
entries.contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the p doubles: slapped, slapping.

entries.meaning: To hit someone or something sharply with an open hand. ---
examples: He smacked the table so hard the glasses jumped.
Her mother never had to smack her twice.
The kid got smacked on the wrist for grabbing.

entries.meaning: To push someone or something roughly and suddenly. ---
examples: Someone shoved me from behind in the crowd.
Don't shove — there is room for everybody.
They were pushing and shoving in front of the gate.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shove him aside), intransitive (stop shoving)
entries.contrast: The o sounds like /ʌ/: SHUV, rhyming with love, not with stove.

entries.meaning: To fight someone by holding them and trying to force them to the ground. ---
examples: Two officers wrestled the gun away from him.
My brother used to wrestle in high school.
They were still wrestling on the floor when help arrived.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wrestle him to the ground), intransitive (he wrestled in college)
entries.contrast: Both the w and the t are silent: RES-ul.

entries.meaning: To fight noisily and without rules, usually in a public place. ---
examples: Fans brawled in the parking lot after the game.
Men who brawl in bars usually end up in a cell.
They were brawling outside when the police pulled up.

entries.meaning: To step heavily on someone or something and crush it. ---
examples: The crowd trampled the fence in the rush to get out.
Cattle will trample a garden in minutes.
Two people were trampled at the entrance.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (trample the flowers), intransitive (trample on his rights)

entries.meaning: To hit someone or something hard again and again. ---
examples: Waves battered the seawall all night.
The wind kept battering the old barn.
She had been battered by her husband for years.

entries.meaning: To fight against something harmful in order to stop it or reduce it. ---
examples: The city combated street crime with more patrols.
New laws are meant to combat online fraud.
They have been combating the same problem for a decade.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one t: combated, combating (British often doubles it).

entries.meaning: Kill has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The crash killed two passengers.
One hard frost can kill every plant in the yard.
Thousands have been killed since the war began.
My feet are killing me.
That hike killed my knees.
Cheap headphones kill my ears after an hour.
The committee killed the bill without a vote.
Kill the engine before you open the hood.
The story was killed an hour before the paper went to press.

senses.head: To make a person, animal, or plant die
examples: The crash killed two passengers.
One hard frost can kill every plant in the yard.
Thousands have been killed since the war began.

senses.head: To cause someone a lot of physical pain
body: (сильно болеть, ныть (о ногах, спине); доставлять сильную боль)
examples: My feet are killing me.
That hike killed my knees.
Cheap headphones kill my ears after an hour.

senses.head: To stop something from going ahead or from running — a plan, a story, or a machine
examples: The committee killed the bill without a vote.
Kill the engine before you open the hood.
The story was killed an hour before the paper went to press.

entries.русский: убивать, убить; сильно болеть, ныть (о ногах, спине); доставлять сильную боль; прекращать, прекратить; зарубить (проект); заглушить (мотор), выключить
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (kill a man), intransitive (smoking kills)

entries.meaning: To kill a person deliberately and unlawfully. ---
examples: He murdered his business partner for the insurance.
Nobody believed she could murder anyone.
The witness had been murdered a week before the trial.

entries.meaning: To murder an important person, usually for political reasons. ---
examples: A gunman assassinated the ambassador in 1974.
Two groups had plotted to assassinate the judge.
The president was assassinated in broad daylight.
entries.contrast: Two double letters: a-ss-a-ss-inate.

entries.meaning: Slaughter has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The invaders slaughtered everyone in the village.
They slaughter the pigs in late autumn.
Whole herds were being slaughtered to stop the disease.
They slaughtered us forty-five to three.
We got slaughtered in the second half.
Any decent team would slaughter us right now.

senses.head: To kill people or animals in large numbers
examples: The invaders slaughtered everyone in the village.
They slaughter the pigs in late autumn.
Whole herds were being slaughtered to stop the disease.

senses.head: To beat an opponent by a huge margin (informal)
examples: They slaughtered us forty-five to three.
We got slaughtered in the second half.
Any decent team would slaughter us right now.

entries.русский: истреблять, устраивать бойню; забивать (скот); разгромить, разнести (в игре, на выборах)
entries.contrast: The gh is silent, and it does not rhyme with laughter: SLAW-tur, LAF-tur.

entries.meaning: To kill a large number of people who cannot defend themselves. ---
examples: Soldiers massacred the prisoners in the courtyard.
No army admits it came to massacre civilians.
The villagers had been massacred days earlier.
entries.contrast: The -cre ending sounds like -ker, and the e drops before -ing: massacring.

entries.meaning: Execute has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The state executed him thirty years after the crime.
No court in that country can execute a minor.
Six prisoners were executed that spring.
The team executed the play perfectly.
Someone has to execute the plan, not just write it.
The order was executed within the hour.

senses.head: To kill someone as a legal punishment
examples: The state executed him thirty years after the crime.
No court in that country can execute a minor.
Six prisoners were executed that spring.

senses.head: To carry out a plan, an order, or a task
examples: The team executed the play perfectly.
Someone has to execute the plan, not just write it.
The order was executed within the hour.

entries.meaning: To cause someone severe pain deliberately, often to force information out of them. ---
examples: Guards tortured him for three days.
No law allows the army to torture prisoners.
He claims he was tortured in that camp.

entries.meaning: To make a bomb explode, or to explode. ---
examples: Engineers detonated the old shell in an empty field.
One wire is enough to detonate the charge.
The device was detonated by remote control.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (detonate a bomb), intransitive (the charge detonated)

entries.meaning: To choose a particular person or place to attack or aim at. ---
examples: The missiles targeted the power station.
Thieves often target houses with no lights on.
Reporters had been targeted by both sides.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: targeted, targeting.

entries.meaning: Arm has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Foreign governments armed both sides of the war.
Nobody wants to arm a militia that cannot be controlled.
The men were armed with rifles and knives.
Arm the alarm before you leave the house.
She armed the security system and locked the door.
The device had already been armed when the squad arrived.

senses.head: To supply a person or group with weapons
examples: Foreign governments armed both sides of the war.
Nobody wants to arm a militia that cannot be controlled.
The men were armed with rifles and knives.

senses.head: To set a weapon or an alarm system so that it is ready to go off
body: (ставить на боевой взвод; ставить на сигнализацию, включать (охрану))
examples: Arm the alarm before you leave the house.
She armed the security system and locked the door.
The device had already been armed when the squad arrived.

entries.русский: вооружать, вооружить; ставить на боевой взвод; ставить на сигнализацию, включать (охрану)

entries.meaning: Disarm has 3 distinct senses.
examples: An officer disarmed him without firing a shot.

The rebels have been disarmed under the agreement.
You have thirty seconds to disarm the alarm.
A robot disarmed the device.
The security system had not been disarmed.

She has a way of disarming people who come in ready to fight.

senses.head: To take weapons away from a person or group, or to give up weapons
examples: An officer disarmed him without firing a shot.
The treaty required both armies to disarm.
The rebels have been disarmed under the agreement.

senses.head: To switch off an alarm system, or to make a bomb safe
examples: You have thirty seconds to disarm the alarm.
A robot disarmed the device.
The security system had not been disarmed.

senses.head: To make someone stop feeling angry or suspicious, usually by being charming or honest
examples: Humor can disarm an angry customer.
His apology disarmed her completely.
She has a way of disarming people who come in ready to fight.

entries.русский: разоружать, разоружить; обезоруживать; отключать, отключить (сигнализацию); обезвреживать, обезвредить (бомбу); обезоруживать, обезоружить; располагать к себе
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (disarm the gunman), intransitive (both sides agreed to disarm)

entries.meaning: Defend has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A hundred men defended the bridge for two days.
She learned to defend herself as a teenager.

senses.head: To protect someone or something from attack
examples: A hundred men defended the bridge for two days.
She learned to defend herself as a teenager.
The town had been defended by volunteers.

senses.head: To compete in order to keep a title or championship you already hold
examples: He will defend his title in Las Vegas this fall.
She defended her Olympic gold four years later.
The club is defending an unbeaten home record.

entries.русский: защищать, защитить; оборонять; защищать титул, отстаивать звание
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (defend the city), intransitive (they fought to defend)
entries.contrast: You defend something against or from an attacker.

entries.meaning: To watch over a place or person in order to keep them safe or stop them escaping. ---
examples: Two soldiers guarded the gate all night.
A dog will guard the yard better than a lock.
The building is being guarded around the clock.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (guard the entrance), intransitive (guard against mistakes)
entries.contrast: Silent u after the g: guard, not "gard".

entries.meaning: To stand between someone and danger so that they are not hurt. ---
examples: He shielded the child with his own body.

The witness was shielded from the cameras.
entries.contrast: Takes from: shield him from the blast.

entries.meaning: Fortify has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The army fortified the hills above the road.
They had three weeks to fortify the camp.
Every village along the border has been fortified.
Most milk sold here is fortified with vitamin D.
They fortified the flour with iron and folic acid.
The program fortifies salt with iodine.

senses.head: To build walls or defenses to make a place stronger against attack
examples: The army fortified the hills above the road.
They had three weeks to fortify the camp.
Every village along the border has been fortified.

senses.head: To add vitamins or minerals to a food or a drink
examples: Most milk sold here is fortified with vitamin D.
They fortified the flour with iron and folic acid.
The program fortifies salt with iodine.

entries.contrast: Consonant plus -y, so y becomes -ie-: fortifies, fortified.

entries.meaning: To move regularly around an area to guard it or watch for trouble. ---
examples: Two jeeps patrolled the perimeter every hour.
Soldiers patrol the border on foot.
Helicopters were patrolling the coast all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (patrol the border), intransitive (guards patrol at night)

entries.meaning: To make someone decide not to do something, usually by threat or fear. ---

entries.contrast: Stress on the last syllable, so the r doubles: deterred, deterring; deter someone from doing something.

The violence in the film repelled her.
His table manners repel everyone in the office.
I was repelled by the smell before I even opened the door.

The spray repelled the mosquitoes all evening.
This fabric is very good at repelling water.

senses.head: To drive an attacking force back and away
examples: The garrison repelled three assaults in one night.
A small force can repel a bigger one from high ground.
The attack was repelled before it reached the wall.

senses.head: To make someone feel strong dislike or disgust
examples: The violence in the film repelled her.
His table manners repel everyone in the office.
I was repelled by the smell before I even opened the door.

senses.head: To push something away by a force, or to keep it from getting in
examples: Two magnets facing the same way repel each other.
The spray repelled the mosquitoes all evening.
This fabric is very good at repelling water.

entries.русский: отражать, отбивать (нападение); вызывать отвращение, отталкивать; отталкивать (о магнитах); отпугивать, не пропускать (воду, насекомых)
entries.contrast: Stress on the last syllable, so the l doubles: repelled, repelling.

entries.meaning: Resist has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The villagers resisted for nearly a month.
He was charged with resisting arrest.
Some of the old families have resisted every change.
I couldn't resist a second slice of cake.
She resisted the urge to answer him.
He has never been good at resisting a bargain.
Stainless steel resists rust better than iron.
The coating resisted the salt water all winter.
We need a fabric capable of resisting heat.

senses.head: To fight against something or refuse to accept it
examples: The villagers resisted for nearly a month.
He was charged with resisting arrest.
Some of the old families have resisted every change.

senses.head: To stop yourself from doing or taking something you want
examples: I couldn't resist a second slice of cake.
She resisted the urge to answer him.
He has never been good at resisting a bargain.

senses.head: For a material to stay undamaged by something that would normally harm it
examples: Stainless steel resists rust better than iron.
The coating resisted the salt water all winter.
We need a fabric capable of resisting heat.

entries.русский: сопротивляться; противостоять; удерживаться от, устоять перед (соблазном); быть устойчивым к, не поддаваться (жару, коррозии)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (resist arrest), intransitive (the town did not resist)
entries.contrast: No preposition: resist the pressure, not "resist to the pressure".

entries.meaning: To stop someone or something from passing or from succeeding. ---
examples: Protesters blocked the main highway for hours.
One senator can block the whole bill.
The road has been blocked since the fighting started.
entries.phrasal verbs: block in · block off · block out · block out

entries.meaning: To turn a blow, a shot, or an attack away from its target. ---
examples: His arm deflected most of the blow.
The minister tried to deflect every hard question.
The shot had been deflected by the door frame.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (deflect a blow), intransitive (the bullet deflected)

entries.meaning: Dodge has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He dodged the first punch and threw one back.
You cannot dodge a bullet, whatever the movies say.
She spent the whole interview dodging the question.
The senator dodged the question twice.
Some firms dodge taxes through offshore accounts.
He spent the whole year dodging his responsibilities.

senses.head: To move quickly aside to avoid being hit
examples: He dodged the first punch and threw one back.
You cannot dodge a bullet, whatever the movies say.
She spent the whole interview dodging the question.

senses.head: To avoid a question, a duty, or a payment by being clever about it
examples: The senator dodged the question twice.
Some firms dodge taxes through offshore accounts.
He spent the whole year dodging his responsibilities.

entries.русский: уворачиваться, увернуться; уклоняться; уклоняться, уклониться (от вопроса, обязанностей, налогов)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dodge the punch), intransitive (he dodged to the left)
entries.contrast: The silent e drops before -ing: dodging, not "dodgeing".

entries.meaning: To give someone a safe place to stay, or to take cover yourself. ---
examples: A church sheltered forty families that winter.
They had nowhere to shelter when the shelling began.
Hundreds were sheltering in the subway stations.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shelter refugees), intransitive (shelter from the shelling)

entries.meaning: To reply to an attack or argument with one of your own. ---
examples: The general countered with an attack on the flank.
Nothing he says can counter that evidence.
They were countering every claim within an hour.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (counter the argument), intransitive ("Not true," he countered)

entries.meaning: To do something harmful to someone because they harmed you first. ---
examples: The other side retaliated within hours.
If we hit them now, they will retaliate.
He was fired for retaliating against a witness.
entries.contrast: Takes against or for: retaliate against a rival, retaliate for the raid.

entries.meaning: To punish someone for a wrong done to you or to a person you care about. ---
examples: He swore he would avenge his brother's death.
The family avenged the insult a year later.
She died believing her son had been avenged.
entries.contrast: Avenge is the verb; revenge is normally the noun: take revenge, but avenge a death.

entries.meaning: To frighten or hurt someone weaker, again and again. ---
examples: Older boys bullied him for two years.
Nobody should have to bully a coworker to get respect.
She was being bullied online every night.
entries.contrast: Consonant plus -y, so y becomes -ie-: bullies, bullied — but bullying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To annoy or attack someone repeatedly over a period of time. ---
examples: Guards harassed the drivers at every checkpoint.
He was accused of harassing two employees.
She has been harassed by phone calls for months.
entries.contrast: One r, two s's, and the third person adds -es: harasses.

entries.meaning: To frighten a person or group badly by using violence or threats. ---
examples: One gang terrorized the whole neighborhood.
They used the dogs to terrorize the prisoners.
The village had been terrorized for a year.
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize: terrorize (British terrorise).

entries.meaning: To force someone to do something by threatening to reveal a secret about them. ---
examples: Someone blackmailed him over the old photographs.
They tried to blackmail the mayor into signing.
He admitted blackmailing two former clients.

entries.meaning: To get money or something else from someone by using threats or force. ---
examples: The gang extorted money from every shop on the block.
They tried to extort a confession out of him.
Thousands had been extorted before anyone complained.
entries.contrast: Takes from: extort money from a shop owner.

entries.meaning: To make someone do something by using force or threats. ---
examples: Officers coerced him into signing the statement.
You cannot coerce a witness and expect the case to stand.
The confession had clearly been coerced.
entries.contrast: Coerce someone into doing something; the oe is two syllables: koh-URS.

entries.meaning: Force has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Hunger forced the defenders to surrender.
Nobody can force you to testify against your husband.
Hundreds of families are being forced out of the valley.
They had to force the door to get her out.
Someone forced the lock on the shed.
The window had been forced from the outside.

senses.head: To make someone do something they do not want to do
examples: Hunger forced the defenders to surrender.
Nobody can force you to testify against your husband.
Hundreds of families are being forced out of the valley.

senses.head: To open something by breaking it or by using physical strength
examples: They had to force the door to get her out.
Someone forced the lock on the shed.
The window had been forced from the outside.

entries.русский: заставлять, заставить; принуждать; взламывать, взломать; выламывать, выломать (дверь, замок)
entries.contrast: Force someone to do something — with to, unlike make someone do.
entries.phrasal verbs: force back · force down · force on · force out

entries.meaning: To try hard to persuade someone to do something they are unwilling to do. ---
examples: His family pressured him into dropping the case.
Don't let them pressure you into an answer today.
Witnesses say they were pressured by both lawyers.
entries.contrast: Pressure someone into doing something, or to do it.

entries.meaning: To treat a person cruelly or violently, or to use power unfairly. ---
examples: He abused his position to silence critics.
No one should abuse an animal like that.
She had been abused as a child.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in /z/ (uh-BYOOZ); the noun abuse ends in /s/ (uh-BYOOS).

entries.meaning: To argue about small, unimportant things. ---
examples: The two of them bickered all the way home.
Neighbors bicker over a foot of fence.
They have been bickering about money since January.
entries.contrast: Takes over or about: bicker over the bill.

entries.meaning: To formally argue that something is wrong, or to compete for something. ---
examples: The family contested the will in court.
He plans to contest the result of the election.
Every inch of that border has been contested for years.
entries.contrast: The verb is kun-TEST; the noun contest is KAHN-test, stressed on the first syllable.

entries.meaning: To say cruel things to someone in order to make them angry or upset. ---
examples: The other players taunted him about the missed shot.
Don't taunt a man who has nothing left to lose.
He was taunting the crowd from the far side of the fence.

entries.meaning: To make fun of someone in a cruel way so that others laugh at them. ---
examples: Newspapers ridiculed the plan for weeks.
It is easy to ridicule an idea you never had to test.
His accent was ridiculed by half the class.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone or something publicly and strongly. ---
examples: The mayor denounced the attack the same evening.
Church leaders continue to denounce the new law.
He was denounced by his own party.

entries.meaning: Condemn has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Both governments condemned the bombing.
It costs nothing to condemn violence in a speech.
He was condemned to death by a military court.
No judge wants to condemn a teenager to life in prison.
The court condemned him to death in 1962.
They were condemned to hard labor.
The city can condemn any building without a fire escape.
Inspectors condemned the old school last spring.
The house has been condemned and will be torn down.

senses.head: To say very strongly that something or someone is wrong or evil
examples: Both governments condemned the bombing.
It costs nothing to condemn violence in a speech.
He was condemned to death by a military court.

senses.head: To give someone a punishment, especially in a court of law
examples: No judge wants to condemn a teenager to life in prison.
The court condemned him to death in 1962.
They were condemned to hard labor.

senses.head: To declare officially that a building is too unsafe to be used
examples: The city can condemn any building without a fire escape.
Inspectors condemned the old school last spring.
The house has been condemned and will be torn down.

entries.русский: осуждать, осудить; приговаривать; приговаривать, приговорить (к); обрекать; признавать аварийным (здание), признать непригодным для жилья
entries.contrast: The final n is silent: kun-DEM — though you hear it in condemnation.

entries.meaning: To treat a group of people cruelly and unfairly, giving them no freedom. ---
examples: That regime oppressed its own people for forty years.
No government admits that it oppresses anyone.
The minority had been oppressed for generations.
entries.contrast: Two p's, two s's, and the third person adds -es: oppresses.

entries.meaning: To face someone or something difficult directly instead of avoiding it. ---
examples: She finally confronted her boss about the missing hours.
Sooner or later you have to confront the problem.
He was confronted by two men in the parking lot.
entries.русский: противостоять; открыто выступать против; смело встречать

entries.meaning: To question whether something is right, or to invite someone to fight or compete. ---
examples: He challenged the ruling in a higher court.
Nobody dared to challenge the old man's authority.
The result is being challenged by three candidates.
entries.contrast: Challenge someone to something: challenged him to a fight.

entries.meaning: Defy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Thousands defied the curfew that night.
Few officers will defy a direct order.
She has defied her family since she was sixteen.
The view from the ridge defies description.
His comeback defied everyone's predictions.
The test results have defied explanation so far.

senses.head: To refuse openly to obey a person, rule, or order
examples: Thousands defied the curfew that night.
Few officers will defy a direct order.
She has defied her family since she was sixteen.

senses.head: To be impossible to explain, describe, or believe
examples: The view from the ridge defies description.
His comeback defied everyone's predictions.
The test results have defied explanation so far.

entries.русский: бросать вызов; открыто не подчиняться; не поддаваться (объяснению, описанию)
entries.contrast: Consonant plus -y, so y becomes -ie-: defies, defied — but defying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: Rally has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Farmers rallied on the steps of the capitol.
He can still rally a crowd in any small town.
The party has rallied behind its new leader.
Stocks usually rally when interest rates fall.
The team rallied from seventeen points down to win.
The market has rallied for three straight weeks.

senses.head: To come together, or bring people together, to support a cause or a leader
examples: Farmers rallied on the steps of the capitol.
He can still rally a crowd in any small town.
The party has rallied behind its new leader.

senses.head: To recover and rise again after a fall in price, strength, or score
examples: Stocks usually rally when interest rates fall.
The team rallied from seventeen points down to win.
The market has rallied for three straight weeks.

entries.русский: собираться на митинг; сплачивать(ся); оживать, восстанавливаться (о рынке, ценах); отыгрываться, отыграться
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (rally supporters), intransitive (the crowd rallied downtown)
entries.contrast: Consonant plus -y: rallies, rallied, but rallying.

entries.meaning: To stand outside a workplace in protest, usually to stop people going in. ---
examples: Nurses picketed the hospital for eleven days.
They plan to picket every store in the chain.
Drivers have been picketing the depot since Monday.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (picket the factory), intransitive (workers picketed all week)
entries.contrast: Stress on the first syllable, so the t stays single: picketed, picketing.

entries.meaning: To refuse to buy from, deal with, or take part in something as a protest. ---
examples: Shoppers boycotted the company for a year.
Two parties plan to boycott the election.
The games were boycotted by a dozen countries.

entries.meaning: To join a violent crowd that fights, breaks things, or attacks the police. ---
examples: Prisoners rioted after the visits were canceled.
Crowds riot when the price of bread doubles.
People had been rioting in the capital for three nights.
entries.contrast: Two syllables, RY-ut, and the t stays single: rioted, rioting.

entries.meaning: To fight against a government or authority, or to refuse to accept its control. ---
examples: The colonies rebelled against the crown.
Teenagers rebel against whatever their parents believe.
Half the army had rebelled by the end of the month.
entries.contrast: The verb is ri-BEL; the noun rebel is REB-ul. Stress on the last syllable doubles the l: rebelled.

entries.meaning: Revolt has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The peasants revolted after the third bad harvest.
Whole provinces may revolt if the tax goes through.
Sailors were revolting in two ports at once.
The smell of the fish revolted her.
Cruelty to animals revolts most people.
I was revolted by what I saw in the video.

senses.head: To rise up violently against a ruler or government
examples: The peasants revolted after the third bad harvest.
Whole provinces may revolt if the tax goes through.
Sailors were revolting in two ports at once.

senses.head: To make someone feel sick or disgusted
examples: The smell of the fish revolted her.
Cruelty to animals revolts most people.
I was revolted by what I saw in the video.

entries.русский: восставать, поднимать восстание; вызывать отвращение, внушать омерзение
entries.contrast: Takes against: revolt against the king.

entries.meaning: To work in an organized way over time to change something or win support. ---
examples: She campaigned for prison reform for twenty years.
They campaign against the pipeline every summer.
He has been campaigning since the spring.
entries.contrast: Silent g: kam-PAYN. Takes for or against.

entries.meaning: To surround a port, road, or country so that nothing can go in or out. ---
examples: Warships blockaded the harbor for six months.
Farmers threatened to blockade the highway with tractors.
The city has been blockaded since the spring.
entries.contrast: Stress on the second syllable: blah-KAYD, unlike the verb block.

entries.meaning: Occupy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Troops occupied the airport within an hour.
Students plan to occupy the administration building.
The country was occupied for four years.
Her family occupies the top two floors.
The meeting occupied the whole morning.
Every seat in the theater was occupied.
A box of crayons will occupy the kids for an hour.
She occupied herself with a crossword while she waited.
He kept the toddler occupied while I cooked.

senses.head: To take control of a place by force and stay there
examples: Troops occupied the airport within an hour.
Students plan to occupy the administration building.
The country was occupied for four years.

senses.head: To live or work in a place, or to fill a space or a period of time
examples: Her family occupies the top two floors.
The meeting occupied the whole morning.
Every seat in the theater was occupied.

senses.head: To keep someone busy
examples: A box of crayons will occupy the kids for an hour.
She occupied herself with a crossword while she waited.
He kept the toddler occupied while I cooked.

entries.русский: оккупировать; занимать (захватив); занимать (помещение, место, время); занимать (кого-л.), развлекать, отвлекать
entries.contrast: Consonant plus -y: occupies, occupied, but occupying.

entries.meaning: To do what a person, law, or order tells you to do. ---
examples: The soldiers obeyed without a word.
You have to obey the same rules as everyone else.
He claimed he was only obeying orders.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (obey an order), intransitive (the dog obeys)
entries.contrast: The y follows a vowel, so it never changes: obeys, obeyed. No preposition: obey the law.

entries.meaning: To refuse to do what you are told to do by a person or law. ---
examples: Two officers disobeyed the order to fire.
Nobody in that unit would dare disobey him.
He was punished for disobeying a direct command.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (disobey an order), intransitive (he disobeyed again)

entries.meaning: To move people out of a dangerous place, or to leave it. ---
examples: The army evacuated four villages near the front.
Families were told to evacuate before dark.
The building had been evacuated an hour earlier.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (evacuate the town), intransitive (residents evacuated at noon)

entries.meaning: Abandon has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The crew abandoned the ship at midnight.
They refused to abandon the wounded.
The position had been abandoned days before.
They abandoned the search when it got dark.
The city has abandoned plans for a new stadium.
He refused to abandon hope of finding her.

senses.head: To leave a place, thing, or person that you are responsible for, and not return
examples: The crew abandoned the ship at midnight.
They refused to abandon the wounded.
The position had been abandoned days before.

senses.head: To give up an activity, a plan, or a belief before it is finished or fulfilled
examples: They abandoned the search when it got dark.
The city has abandoned plans for a new stadium.
He refused to abandon hope of finding her.

entries.русский: покидать, покинуть; бросать, бросить; отказываться от, отказаться от; бросать, забросить (дело)
entries.contrast: The final n does not double: abandoned, not "abandonned".

entries.meaning: To leave the army without permission, or to leave someone who needs you. ---
examples: Half the regiment deserted that winter.
A man who would desert his friends will desert you too.
He was shot for deserting his post.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (desert your post), intransitive (two men deserted)
entries.contrast: The verb is di-ZURT; the noun desert (the Sahara) is DEZ-urt.

entries.meaning: To join the armed forces, or to get someone's help. ---
examples: My grandfather enlisted in 1942.
Thousands enlist every year straight out of school.
She has enlisted two neighbors to help with the petition.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (he enlisted at eighteen), transitive (enlist their support)

entries.meaning: Deploy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The general deployed two brigades along the river.
They may deploy more troops by the weekend.
He has been deployed overseas three times.
The airbags deploy only in a serious crash.
His parachute deployed at two thousand feet.
The side airbag had not deployed.

senses.head: To move soldiers or equipment into position for action
examples: The general deployed two brigades along the river.
They may deploy more troops by the weekend.
He has been deployed overseas three times.

senses.head: To open out suddenly and go into operation, as an airbag or a parachute does
body: (срабатывать, сработать (о подушке безопасности); раскрываться, раскрыться (о парашюте))
examples: The airbags deploy only in a serious crash.
His parachute deployed at two thousand feet.
The side airbag had not deployed.

entries.русский: развёртывать, размещать (войска); срабатывать, сработать (о подушке безопасности); раскрываться, раскрыться (о парашюте)
entries.contrast: The y follows a vowel, so it stays: deployed, deploying.

entries.meaning: Command has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She commanded a unit of two hundred men.
He can command a room without raising his voice.
The ship was commanded by an officer of twenty-six.
Few teachers command that kind of respect.
The painting commanded four million dollars at auction.
Her work has commanded attention since her first show.

senses.head: To be in charge of soldiers, or to order someone to do something
examples: She commanded a unit of two hundred men.
He can command a room without raising his voice.
The ship was commanded by an officer of twenty-six.

senses.head: To be important or valuable enough to get respect, attention, or a high price
examples: Few teachers command that kind of respect.
The painting commanded four million dollars at auction.
Her work has commanded attention since her first show.

entries.русский: командовать; приказывать; вызывать (уважение), пользоваться (авторитетом); стоить (о цене)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (command a regiment), intransitive (he was born to command)
entries.contrast: The a is /æ/ as in hand: kuh-MAND, not "kuh-MAHND".

entries.meaning: To gather soldiers or supporters and make them ready for action. ---
examples: The country mobilized within forty-eight hours.
Both sides are trying to mobilize young voters.
Reserves had already been mobilized by then.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (mobilize the reserves), intransitive (the army mobilized)
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize: mobilize (British mobilise).

entries.meaning: Betray has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A neighbor betrayed the family to the soldiers.
He would never betray the people who hid him.
She felt betrayed by everyone in the office.
His face betrays nothing.
Her voice betrayed how nervous she was.
A slight tremor in his hands had betrayed him.

senses.head: To harm someone who trusts you, especially by helping their enemies
examples: A neighbor betrayed the family to the soldiers.
He would never betray the people who hid him.
She felt betrayed by everyone in the office.

senses.head: To show a feeling you were trying to hide, without meaning to
examples: His face betrays nothing.
Her voice betrayed how nervous she was.
A slight tremor in his hands had betrayed him.

entries.русский: предавать, предать; выдавать; выдавать, выдать (чувства); обнаруживать
entries.contrast: The y follows a vowel, so it stays: betrayed, betraying.

entries.meaning: Conspire has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Four officers conspired to overthrow the government.
Nobody could prove the two men conspire at all.
They were charged with conspiring against the state.
Bad weather and a flat tire conspired to ruin the trip.
Everything seems to conspire against us on moving day.
Traffic, rain, and a late train were conspiring to make him miss the wedding.

senses.head: To plan something harmful or illegal secretly with other people
examples: Four officers conspired to overthrow the government.
Nobody could prove the two men conspire at all.
They were charged with conspiring against the state.

senses.head: Of events or conditions, to seem to combine to produce a bad result
examples: Bad weather and a flat tire conspired to ruin the trip.
Everything seems to conspire against us on moving day.
Traffic, rain, and a late train were conspiring to make him miss the wedding.

entries.русский: сговариваться, устраивать заговор; складываться неудачно (об обстоятельствах), сойтись
entries.contrast: Takes against or with, and to do something: conspired to kill him.

entries.meaning: Plot has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Two generals plotted to seize the capital.
Prisoners plot escapes they will never attempt.
He had been plotting against his own brother.
Plot the results on a graph.
The navigator plotted a course around the storm.
Every case has been plotted on a city map.

senses.head: To make a secret plan to do something harmful
examples: Two generals plotted to seize the capital.
Prisoners plot escapes they will never attempt.
He had been plotting against his own brother.

senses.head: To mark points or a route on a graph, a chart, or a map
examples: Plot the results on a graph.
The navigator plotted a course around the storm.
Every case has been plotted on a city map.

entries.русский: замышлять, готовить заговор; наносить на график, строить (график); прокладывать, проложить (курс)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (plot a coup), intransitive (they plotted for months)
entries.contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the t doubles: plotted, plotting.

entries.meaning: To set a place or people free from an enemy or from control. ---
examples: Allied troops liberated the city in August.
No army can liberate a country against its will.
The camp was liberated a week before the war ended.

entries.meaning: To join with another person or country for a shared purpose, usually against someone. ---
examples: Two small states allied against their neighbor.
He chose to ally himself with the reformers.
The country had long been allied with Britain.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (ally yourself with them), intransitive (the tribes allied)
entries.contrast: The verb is uh-LY; the noun ally is AL-eye. Y becomes -ie-: allies, allied.

entries.meaning: To join people or groups together so that they act as one. ---
examples: The invasion united parties that had hated each other.
Nothing will unite that town again.
The factions are uniting behind a single candidate.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (a threat unites people), intransitive (the parties united)
entries.contrast: Begins with a /j/ sound: yoo-NYT, so it takes a, not an.

entries.meaning: Subdue has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Three officers subdued the man on the platform.
It took a year to subdue the last of the rebels.
He was subdued and handcuffed within seconds.
She subdued her anger and answered politely.
Soft lighting can subdue the mood of a whole room.
The music was subdued so that guests could hear each other.

senses.head: To bring a person or group under control by force
examples: Three officers subdued the man on the platform.
It took a year to subdue the last of the rebels.
He was subdued and handcuffed within seconds.

senses.head: To make a feeling, a sound, or a color less strong
examples: She subdued her anger and answered politely.
Soft lighting can subdue the mood of a whole room.
The music was subdued so that guests could hear each other.

entries.русский: усмирять, подавлять; одолевать; приглушать, приглушить; сдерживать, подавлять (чувство)
entries.contrast: The silent e drops before -ing: subduing.

entries.meaning: To hold someone back physically, or to stop yourself from acting. ---
examples: Two friends restrained him before he swung again.
Try to restrain yourself when he starts shouting.
The suspect was restrained on the ground.

entries.meaning: To stop a protest, a report, or a feeling by force or authority. ---
examples: Troops suppressed the uprising in a single day.
Governments that suppress the press rarely stop there.
The report had been suppressed for two years.
entries.contrast: Two p's and two s's; the third person adds -es: suppresses.

entries.meaning: To treat people cruelly over a long time because of their race, religion, or beliefs. ---
examples: The empire persecuted Christians for three centuries.
Any state can persecute a minority and call it order.
They were persecuted until they finally left the country.
entries.contrast: Persecute (преследовать, притеснять) is not prosecute (привлекать к суду).

entries.meaning: To take someone to a police station because they are suspected of a crime. ---
examples: Police arrested four people at the protest.
They can arrest you for that in this state.
He has been arrested twice this year.
entries.contrast: Takes for: arrested for theft.

entries.meaning: Detain has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Border guards detained him for six hours.
They can detain a suspect for two days without charges.
Dozens are still being detained without trial.
I won't detain you long.
A long phone call detained him at the office.
We were detained by traffic and missed the first act.

senses.head: To keep someone in official custody and not let them leave
examples: Border guards detained him for six hours.
They can detain a suspect for two days without charges.
Dozens are still being detained without trial.

senses.head: To keep someone from leaving or going on, so that they are late
examples: I won't detain you long.
A long phone call detained him at the office.
We were detained by traffic and missed the first act.

entries.русский: задерживать, задержать; заключать под стражу; задерживать, задержать (кого-л.), отнимать время

entries.meaning: To put someone in prison and keep them there. ---
examples: The regime imprisoned hundreds of journalists.
You cannot imprison a man for what he thinks.
He was imprisoned for eleven years.
entries.русский: заключать в тюрьму, сажать в тюрьму
entries.contrast: The final n does not double: imprisoned, imprisoning.

entries.meaning: To put someone in jail as a punishment. ---
examples: The court jailed him for five years.
They rarely jail first offenders here.
She was jailed for refusing to name her source.
entries.русский: сажать в тюрьму, заключать под стражу

entries.meaning: To question someone closely and for a long time, often in an aggressive way. ---
examples: Agents interrogated him through the night.
They plan to interrogate every man on the list.
He was being interrogated when his lawyer arrived.
entries.contrast: Double r: interrogate.

entries.meaning: To officially charge someone with a crime and take them to court. ---
examples: The city prosecuted him for assault.
They decided not to prosecute the driver.
Trespassers will be prosecuted.
entries.русский: привлекать к суду, преследовать в судебном порядке
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (prosecute a case), intransitive (the state declined to prosecute)

entries.meaning: To decide officially in court that someone is guilty of a crime. ---
examples: The jury convicted him in under an hour.
It is hard to convict anyone on that evidence.
She has never been convicted of anything.
entries.contrast: The verb is kun-VIKT; the noun convict (a prisoner) is KAHN-vikt. Takes of: convicted of fraud.

entries.meaning: To take legal action against a person or company in a court. ---
examples: He sued his employer for wrongful dismissal.
If they print that, she will sue.
The city is being sued by three families.
entries.русский: подавать в суд на, судиться с
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (sue the company), intransitive (they threatened to sue)
entries.contrast: Keep the u but drop the e before -ing: suing, not "sueing".

entries.meaning: To make sure that a law or rule is obeyed. ---
examples: Nobody enforced the curfew in the old town.
It is one thing to pass a law and another to enforce it.
The ban is being enforced for the first time.

entries.meaning: Violate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Both sides violated the ceasefire within a week.
That order would violate international law.
He was arrested for violating the restraining order.
Searching her phone would violate her privacy.
Vandals violated several graves in the old cemetery.
She felt violated for weeks after the break-in.

senses.head: To break a law, rule, or agreement
examples: Both sides violated the ceasefire within a week.
That order would violate international law.
He was arrested for violating the restraining order.

senses.head: To intrude on someone's privacy or body, or on a place people treat as sacred
examples: Searching her phone would violate her privacy.
Vandals violated several graves in the old cemetery.
She felt violated for weeks after the break-in.

entries.русский: нарушать, нарушить (закон, договор); посягать на, нарушать (неприкосновенность); вторгаться

entries.meaning: To help two sides in a conflict reach an agreement. ---
examples: A retired judge mediated the dispute.
Neighbors asked the church to mediate between them.
The talks were mediated by two foreign ministers.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (mediate a dispute), intransitive (she agreed to mediate)
entries.contrast: Takes between: mediate between the two sides.

entries.meaning: To become involved in a conflict in order to change what is happening. ---
examples: A passerby intervened before it turned into a fight.
Nobody expects the army to intervene now.
Two governments have been intervening on opposite sides.
entries.contrast: Takes in or between: intervene in the conflict.

entries.meaning: Escalate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The argument escalated into a brawl.
One more raid could escalate the whole thing.
Tensions have been escalating since the election.
If the agent can't help, ask her to escalate the ticket.
I escalated the complaint to a supervisor.
The case has been escalated to the legal department.

senses.head: To become more serious or violent, or to make something do so
examples: The argument escalated into a brawl.
One more raid could escalate the whole thing.
Tensions have been escalating since the election.

senses.head: To pass a problem to someone with more authority so that it gets solved
examples: If the agent can't help, ask her to escalate the ticket.
I escalated the complaint to a supervisor.
The case has been escalated to the legal department.

entries.русский: обостряться, нарастать; обострять; передавать выше (по инстанции), эскалировать (обращение)
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the fight escalated), transitive (escalate the conflict)
entries.contrast: Takes into: escalated into a war.

entries.meaning: To make a bomb safe, or to make a dangerous situation calmer. ---
examples: A team defused the device in the parking garage.
One calm officer can defuse a crowd like that.
The crisis was defused by a phone call.
entries.contrast: Defuse (обезвредить) is not diffuse (рассеивать).

entries.meaning: Struggle has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She struggled with the man until he let go.
They still struggle for basic rights in that region.
He has been struggling against the ruling for years.
Some students struggle with word problems.
She struggled to pay rent last winter.
The team has been struggling all season.

senses.head: To fight hard against someone or something, especially when you are losing
examples: She struggled with the man until he let go.
They still struggle for basic rights in that region.
He has been struggling against the ruling for years.

senses.head: To find something very difficult to do
body: (с трудом справляться, испытывать трудности; еле справляться)
examples: Some students struggle with word problems.
She struggled to pay rent last winter.
The team has been struggling all season.

entries.русский: бороться; с трудом справляться; с трудом справляться, испытывать трудности; еле справляться
entries.contrast: Takes with, against, or for: struggle against the current.

entries.meaning: To catch someone in a place or situation they cannot get out of. ---
examples: The fire trapped twelve people on the third floor.
They planned to trap the patrol in the canyon.
Two soldiers were trapped behind enemy lines for a month.
entries.contrast: One short vowel plus one consonant, so the p doubles: trapped, trapping.

entries.meaning: To take control of a plane, ship, or truck by force. ---
examples: Four men hijacked the plane over the Atlantic.
Thieves often hijack trucks on that stretch of road.
The bus was hijacked twenty miles from the border.

entries.meaning: To take a person away by force and hold them, usually for money. ---
examples: Gunmen kidnapped two engineers near the port.
They threatened to kidnap his daughter.
He was kidnapped on his way home from work.
entries.contrast: The p doubles in American English: kidnapped, kidnapping.

entries.meaning: To steal things from shops or homes during a war or riot. ---
examples: Crowds looted every store on the avenue.
Soldiers are not supposed to loot the towns they take.
The museum had already been looted.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (loot a store), intransitive (crowds were looting)

entries.meaning: To make a crowd break up and go away, or to break up and go away. ---
examples: Police dispersed the protesters with tear gas.
The crowd refused to disperse.
By midnight everyone had dispersed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (disperse the crowd), intransitive (the crowd dispersed)

entries.meaning: To leave your country or party and join the opposing one.
examples: A colonel defected two days before the offensive.
Dozens of officials defect every year.
He has defected to the other side and taken the files with him.
entries.русский: перебегать (к врагу), дезертировать; бежать из страны
entries.contrast: The verb is di-FEKT; the noun defect (a flaw) is DEE-fekt. Takes to: defected to the West.
